title: Highest-Protein Seeds: Ranking per 100 Grams and per Ounce

seo.title: Highest-Protein Seeds per Serving
seo.meta_description: Compare hemp, pumpkin, sunflower, flax, sesame and chia by protein per 100 grams and per 1-ounce serving.
seo.search_intent: Compare edible seeds by protein concentration and serving.

excerpt: Hemp and pumpkin seeds can nearly match chicken breast for protein when everything is compared per 100 grams. The difference shows up on the plate: seed servings are usually around an ounce and provide roughly 5–9 grams.
content_html:
One number makes seeds look almost unbelievable: hulled hemp and pumpkin seeds are around 30 grams of protein per 100 grams, close to cooked chicken breast. The number is real; it just needs a second line of context.

Most people do not eat five ounces of seeds as the center of dinner. A normal serving is closer to 1 ounce, so this category makes a clean distinction between protein concentration and protein in the amount you actually eat.

The ranking by weight and by serving

SeedProtein/100 gProtein/1 oz
Hulled hemp31.6 g8.8 g
Pumpkin kernels30.2 g8.5 g
Sunflower kernels20.8 g5.8 g
Flaxseed18.3 g5.1 g
Sesame17.7 g5.0 g
Chia16.5 g4.6 g

Hemp and pumpkin really do stand out

Hulled hemp provides 31.6 g protein/100 g and pumpkin seeds 30.2 g. Those are unusually high numbers for plant foods.

Serving size changes the meaning: one ounce of hemp gives about 8.8 g protein, while a 5-ounce chicken breast provides about 44 g. Seeds are concentrated, but they usually work as an addition rather than the whole protein anchor.

Sunflower still contributes a useful amount

Sunflower kernels contain about 20.8 g protein/100 g and nearly 6 g per ounce, along with vitamin E, copper and unsaturated fat.

Flax and chia have another claim to fame

Flax is about 18.3 g protein/100 g and chia about 16.5 g. Their fiber numbers are even more striking: chia is roughly 34 g/100 g and flax around 27 g.

A 20 g serving of chia supplies about 3.3 g protein and 6.8 g fiber; flax provides about 3.7 g protein and 5.4 g fiber. In a spoonful, fiber can be the more remarkable number.

Sesame and tahini

Sesame seeds contain about 17.7 g protein/100 g. Tahini retains a substantial amount after grinding, although brands differ with roasting and formulation.

Why seeds are not “lean protein”

Most seeds exceed 500 calories/100 g because they are rich in fat. Hemp is around 550 calories with 31.6 g protein, compared with cooked chicken breast at about 165 calories with 31 g.

Nearly identical protein by weight, more than three times the energy. That does not make seeds worse foods; it means their package also includes fat, minerals and, depending on the seed, a lot of fiber.

Where they fit naturally

An ounce can add roughly 5–9 g protein to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, sauces or a legume-based meal. That supporting role is where seeds are especially easy to use.

The useful takeaway

Hemp and pumpkin seeds clearly lead on protein concentration. Sunflower, flax, sesame and chia provide less, with other nutritional strengths. Per 100 grams seeds can look like a main protein; per serving they usually make the most sense as a powerful addition.

faq.question: Which seed has the most protein?
faq.answer: Hulled hemp is about 31.6 g/100 g and pumpkin seeds about 30.2 g/100 g.

faq.question: How much protein is in one ounce of seeds?
faq.answer: Hemp provides about 8.8 g, pumpkin 8.5 g and sunflower about 5.8 g.

faq.question: Is chia high in protein?
faq.answer: It contains about 16.5 g/100 g and is even more notable for fiber at roughly 34 g/100 g.
